entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
François Vatable (died March 26, 1547) was a pivotal French humanist scholar, renowned for his profound expertise in Hellenistic Greek and Hebrew studies during the early 16th century. Operating primarily within the intellectual ferment of Paris, Vatable significantly contributed to the burgeoning field of biblical philology, providing critical linguistic groundwork for the Protestant Reformation's emphasis on original scriptural texts. His work, though often collaborative and posthumously published, positioned him as a central figure in the Parisian intellectual circles that sought to reclaim and re-interpret ancient texts through rigorous linguistic analysis.

Vatable's most enduring contribution was his role as Professor of Hebrew at the Collège Royal (later the Collège de France) in Paris, a position he held from 1531 until his death. His lectures attracted a wide array of students, including prominent Reformers like Peter Martyr Vermigli, and were instrumental in disseminating advanced knowledge of Hebrew among European scholars. While Vatable himself published little during his lifetime, his extensive marginal notes and oral teachings were meticulously compiled by his students, notably Robert Estienne, who incorporated Vatable's Hebrew scholarship into his influential 1545 Latin Bible. This edition, featuring Vatable's critical annotations on the Hebrew text, became a standard reference for generations of biblical scholars, both Catholic and Protestant.

entities.summary:
François Vatable (1495, Gamaches – March 26, 1547, Paris) was a pivotal French humanist scholar and Hebraist whose meticulous philological work on the Old Testament profoundly influenced biblical scholarship during the tumultuous era of the Reformation. As a leading professor of Hebrew at the newly established Collège Royal in Paris from 1530, Vatable stood at the forefront of the burgeoning interest in original biblical languages, advocating for a return to the Hebrew text of the Old Testament amidst an intellectual landscape dominated by the Latin Vulgate. His scholarly rigor and dedication to textual accuracy positioned him as a central figure in the Parisian intellectual circles that sought to reconcile classical learning with Christian theology, shaping the methodologies of future generations of biblical exegetes.

Vatable's primary contribution lay in his critical annotations to the Old Testament, particularly his work on the Hebrew text, which were incorporated into Robert Estienne's monumental Latin Vulgate edition of 1545. These annotations, known as the 'Vatablus notes,' offered variant readings, grammatical explanations, and contextual insights derived directly from the Hebrew, providing scholars with an invaluable tool for understanding the original scripture. Though he published little under his own name, his lectures and scholarly discussions were widely circulated through his students and collaborators, making his philological expertise accessible to a broader audience of humanists, theologians, and reformers across Europe. He was also instrumental in promoting the study of Greek, further broadening access to original New Testament texts.
